content.text: CCNA 200-301 STUDY MANUAL
Chapter 17
Internet Protocol Version 6 (IPv6)

This document replaces Chapter 17 of Todd Lammle, CCNA Certification Study Guide, Volume 2, Exam 200-301 (Sybex, 2020), book pages 465 to 494. It covers why IPv6 exists, address format and shortening, address types, special addresses, manual addressing, EUI-64 and stateless autoconfiguration, DHCPv6, the IPv6 header, ICMPv6 and neighbor discovery, and IPv6 static routing, with configuration and verification. Every difference from the book is tagged and listed in the Changes and Gaps Log.

WHAT THE BOOK SAYS
Learning objectives (from the book). After this chapter you should be able to:
Configure and verify IPv6 addressing and prefix (objective 1.8).
Compare IPv6 address types: global unicast, unique local, link local, anycast, multicast and modified EUI-64 (objective 1.9 a to f).
Configure and verify IPv4 and IPv6 static routing (objective 3.3).
VERIFY

Verification note. Every address calculation in this chapter (EUI-64, shortening, expansion, address type, solicited-node multicast, sizes, header bits) was done with a Python script using the ipaddress module and compared with the manual method. The script agreed with the book's EUI-64 examples and found errors in the book's flow label size and one documentation prefix (see the Gaps Log). Nothing in this document was run on real Cisco hardware or in Packet Tracer. Commands and outputs are copied from the book or written from documentation, so they are marked CHECK where they matter.

Book pages 467. BOOK

IPv4 has only about 4.3 billion addresses (2^32). CIDR, VLSM and NAT stretched them, but they were never a real fix. IPv6 was created as the long-term solution: its address is 128 bits, which gives 2^128, about 3.4 x 10^38, addresses (checked by script).
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

The book's numbers are out of date (page 467: "about 7 billion people", "just under half connected", "we will run out within a few years", and a comment about China being barely online). The real situation: IANA gave out its last free IPv4 blocks in February 2011. APNIC ran out in April 2011, ARIN in September 2015, and RIPE NCC in November 2019. IPv4 addresses now come from transfers, leasing or tiny leftover pools. UPDATED Sources: secondary summaries and an APNIC report (see Sources). CHECK
WHY THIS MATTERS
The real driver is not just "more addresses". It is that every device can have its own globally unique address again, without NAT breaking end-to-end connections.
Quick check 17.1
Q1. How many bits is an IPv6 address, and how many bits is an IPv4 address?
Answer: 128 and 32 - The IPv6 space is 2^96 times larger, not four times larger.
Q2. Roughly how many IPv6 addresses exist?
Answer: About 3.4 x 10^38 - 2^128, calculated by script.

sections.title: 17.2 The Benefits and Uses of IPv6

content.text: Book pages 467 to 469. BOOK
| Benefit | What it means |
| Huge address space | 128-bit addresses, more levels of hierarchy, easier route summarisation. |
| Simpler, faster header | Fixed 40-byte header with 8 fields. Rarely used information moves to optional extension headers. |
| No broadcasts | Replaced by multicast and a new type, anycast. This removes IPv4 broadcast storms and the interruptions broadcasts cause. |
| Autoconfiguration | Hosts can build their own address from a router advertisement (plug and play). |
| Multiple addresses per interface | An interface normally has a link-local address and at least one other address. |
| Security built in | The book says IPsec is a mandatory standard feature. See the update below. |
| Expanded multicast | More efficient: only interested hosts process the traffic. |
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

IPsec is no longer mandatory. The book says IPsec is a "standard and mandatory" part of IPv6 (page 468). That was true of the original node requirements (RFC 4294), but RFC 6434 (2011) relaxed support for the IPsec architecture to SHOULD. A later RFC (8504) updated the node requirements again; it was not re-read here. This also matters for book review question 8 (see the Gaps Log). UPDATED Source: secondary summary plus the RFC errata page showing RFC 4294 is obsolete. CHECK
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE
The book also says the address is "four times bigger". It has four times as many bits, but 2^96 times as many addresses. UPDATED (script)
Quick check 17.2
Q1. What replaces broadcast in IPv6?
A. Unicast only
B. Multicast (and anycast is new)
C. ARP
D. Nothing replaces it
Answer: B - There is no broadcast in IPv6.
Q2. How long is the basic IPv6 header?
Answer: 40 bytes, fixed - IPv4 is 20 bytes minimum and variable.
Book pages 469 to 473. BOOK
An IPv6 address is 128 bits, written as eight groups of four hexadecimal digits separated by colons. Each group is 16 bits. Hex digits are 0 to 9 and a to f (not case sensitive).
Book Figure 17.1, example address
| Part | Bits | In the example | Meaning |
| Global routing prefix | 48 | 2001:0db8:3c4d | Given to a site by an ISP (a /48 is common). |
| Subnet ID | 16 | 0012 | Your own subnets: 2^16 = 65,536 /64 subnets from one /48 (script). |
| Interface ID | 64 | 0000:0000:1234:56ab | Identifies the host on the subnet. |
MEMORY TIP
Think /48 from the ISP + 16 bits of subnet = /64 for each LAN. Almost every LAN in IPv6 is a /64. SLAAC needs a /64.
17.3.1 Shortened Expression
Two rules let you shorten an address. BOOK
- Drop leading zeros in each group. 0012 becomes 12, 0000 becomes 0, 0db8 becomes db8. You may not drop trailing zeros (1200 is not 12).
- Replace one contiguous run of all-zero groups with ::. You may use :: only once in an address.
| Step | Address |
| Rule 1 (leading zeros) | 2001:db8:3c4d:12:0:0:1234:56ab |

Why only once? If you wrote 2001::12::1234:56ab, the device cannot know how many zero groups go in each gap. So with two separate zero runs you can compress only one. For 2001:0000:0000:0012:0000:0000:1234:56ab the best the book offers is 2001::12:0:0:1234:56ab.
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

Which run to compress (RFC 5952 recommendation): compress the longest run of zero groups; if two runs are the same length, compress the first one. The script (Python ipaddress) gave 2001::12:0:0:1234:56ab for the book's example, which matches. The exam usually accepts any legal form, but this is the standard way. CHECK RFC 5952 was not re-read; this comes from general knowledge and the script.

How to expand ::: count the groups you can see, subtract from 8, and fill that many zero groups where :: is. For 2001:db8::1 there are 3 visible groups, so 5 zero groups fit in the gap: 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001.
Practice (answers calculated by script)
| Full address | Shortest form |
Prefix length
Like CIDR, IPv6 writes the network part as address/prefix-length, for example 2001:db8:3c4d:12::/64 means the first 64 bits are the network. The remaining 64 bits are the interface ID. ADDED
Quick check 17.3.1
Q1. Is 2001::12::1234:56ab a legal address?
Answer: No - :: can be used only once.
Answer: fe80::204:61ff:fe9d:f156 - Drop leading zeros, then compress the one run of zero groups.
Q3. How many hex digits are in each group and how many bits?
Answer: 4 digits, 16 bits - Eight groups x 16 bits = 128 bits.
17.3.2 Address Types
IPv6 has unicast, multicast and anycast. There is no broadcast. BOOK
| Type | Prefix | Starts with | Delivered to | Routable? |
| Global unicast | 2000::/3 | 2 or 3 | One interface (public) | Yes, on the Internet |
| Link-local unicast | FE80::/10 | fe80 to febf | One interface on the local link | No, never routed |
| Unique local unicast | FC00::/7 | fc or fd | One interface (private) | Within a site or organisation, not on the Internet |
| Multicast | FF00::/8 | ff | All interfaces in the group | Depends on scope |
| Anycast | From a unicast range | Any unicast address | The nearest device sharing the address | Yes (it is a unicast address configured on several devices) |
The first-digit and range values above were calculated by script: FE80::/10 covers fe80:: to febf::, FC00::/7 covers fc00:: to fdff::, and 2000::/3 covers 2000:: to 3fff::.
Global unicast (2000::/3)

The public, routable addresses, like public IPv4. Figure 17.2: a registry gives an ISP a prefix (around /23 to /32), the ISP gives a company a /48 (or similar), the company uses 16 bits for subnets (/64 each) and the last 64 bits identify the host. BOOK
Link-local (FE80::/10)
Like APIPA in IPv4, but far more important. The book says they are used for temporary or local networks and are not routed. Every IPv6-enabled interface gets one automatically. BOOK
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

Why link-local matters more than the book says. Routers use link-local addresses as next hops, and neighbor discovery and routing protocol neighbours use them. With only a link-local address (ipv6 enable) a device can talk only on its own link. ADDED (general knowledge) CHECK
Unique local (FC00::/7)

Replaces the old site-local addresses, which were deprecated in September 2004. They work like IPv4 private addresses: usable inside a site or between sites, not routed on the Internet. The book calls them "nearly globally unique". BOOK
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

In practice only FD00::/8 is used. FC00::/7 is split in two: fc00::/8 is reserved for a possible future registry, and fd00::/8 is the half you generate yourself, with a random 40-bit global ID (for example fd12:3456:789a::/48). The book never says this. UPDATED Source: general knowledge of RFC 4193; the script confirms fd00::/8 sits inside fc00::/7. CHECK
Multicast (FF00::/8)
One-to-many. Always starts with FF. Hosts that have joined the group receive the packet. BOOK
| Address | Group |
| FF02::1 | All nodes on the link (used for RA) |
| FF02::2 | All routers on the link (used for RS) |
| FF02::5 | OSPFv3 all SPF routers |
| FF02::6 | OSPFv3 designated routers |
| FF02::9 | RIPng routers |
| FF02::A | EIGRP routers |
| FF02::1:2 | All DHCPv6 relay agents and servers |
| FF02::1:FFxx:xxxx | Solicited-node multicast (neighbor discovery, see 17.4.5) |
FF02::1 and FF02::2 are in the book. The other rows are ADDED from general knowledge and must be confirmed. CHECK
MEMORY TIP
Hosts send RS to FF02::2 (all routers). Routers send RA to FF02::1 (all nodes). The ending digit is the clue: 1 = nodes, 2 = routers.
Anycast

The same address is configured on several devices and a packet goes to the nearest one by routing distance (one-to-nearest). Anycast addresses are configured on routers or servers, never as a source address. The IETF reserved the top 128 addresses of each /64 for anycast. BOOK
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

Subnet-router anycast. In every subnet the address with an interface ID of all zeros (for example 2001:db8:3c4d:12::) is reserved as the subnet-router anycast address. That is why IOS rejects ipv6 address 2001:db8:3c4d:12::/64 without eui-64 (see 17.6). ADDED CHECK
EXAM CRITICAL
An interface can have several IPv6 addresses at once (link-local plus global plus unique local). Having a global address does not remove the link-local one.
Quick check 17.3.2
Q1. Which prefix is global unicast?
Answer: C - 2000::/3 (addresses starting with 2 or 3).
Q2. Can a router forward a packet whose destination is FE80::1?
Answer: No - Link-local is never routed off the link.
Q3. Which is the Layer 3 delivery model of anycast?
Answer: One-to-nearest - Not one-to-many.
Q4. What kind of address is fd12:3456:789a::1?
Answer: Unique local - It is inside FC00::/7 (script).
17.3.3 Special Addresses
Book Table 17.1, with corrections. BOOK
| Address | Meaning | Note |
| :: (0:0:0:0:0:0:0:0) | Unspecified, like IPv4 0.0.0.0. The source before an address is assigned (DHCPv6 stateful). | BOOK |
| ::1 | Loopback, like IPv4 127.0.0.1. | BOOK |

| ::192.168.100.1 | Book: IPv4 address in a mixed network. | UPDATED This is the old IPv4-compatible format, which is deprecated. Dual-stack sockets use IPv4-mapped addresses written ::ffff:192.168.100.1. |
| 2000::/3 | Global unicast range. | BOOK |
| FC00::/7 | Unique local range. | BOOK |
| FE80::/10 | Link-local range. | BOOK |
| FF00::/8 | Multicast range. | BOOK |
| 3FFF:FFFF::/32 | Book: reserved for documentation. | UPDATED Wrong. See the box below. |
| 2001:0DB8::/32 | Reserved for documentation (RFC 3849). | BOOK |
| 2002::/16 | 6to4 tunnelling (IPv4-to-IPv6 transition). | UPDATED 6to4 is deprecated. Still appears on old exams. |
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

Documentation prefix correction. The book (page 472) lists 3FFF:FFFF::/32 as reserved for documentation. The IANA registry entry is 3fff::/20 (RFC 9637, August 2024, in addition to 2001:db8::/32). The script shows 3fff:ffff::/32 is not inside 3fff::/20, so the book's value is just ordinary global unicast space. Use 2001:db8::/32 in examples, as the book does for all its configs. UPDATED Source: RFC 9637 (official IETF text). 6to4 deprecation: general knowledge, not re-verified. CHECK
WHAT THE BOOK SAYS
Dual-stack: running IPv4 and IPv6 at the same time on a router or host. BOOK The book gives it one line; it is the most common migration method (see the migration note in 17.4.5).
Quick check 17.3.3
Q1. What is the IPv6 loopback address?
Answer: ::1 - There is only one loopback address.
Q2. Which prefix should you use in documentation and labs?
Answer: 2001:db8::/32 - Never real prefixes. 3fff::/20 is also reserved.

sections.title: 17.4 How IPv6 Works in an Internetwork

content.text: Book pages 473 to 483. BOOK
17.4.1 Manual Address Assignment
A Cisco router does not forward IPv6 by default, and no interface has IPv6 enabled until you configure it. First turn on IPv6 routing globally, then address each interface. BOOK
The three ways to give an interface IPv6 (use ONE per address) CHECK
Corp(config)# ipv6 unicast-routing
Corp(config)# interface fastethernet0/0
Corp(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:3c4d:1::1/64
Corp(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:3c4d:1::/64 eui-64
Corp(config-if)# ipv6 enable
- ipv6 unicast-routing (global) enables IPv6 packet forwarding on the router. Without it the router will not route IPv6.
- ipv6 address 2001:db8:3c4d:1::1/64 sets the whole 128-bit address by hand. The /64 is the prefix length.
- ipv6 address 2001:db8:3c4d:1::/64 eui-64 gives only the prefix. The router builds the last 64 bits from the interface MAC (EUI-64).
- ipv6 enable turns IPv6 on using only a link-local address, with no global address. The device then talks only on its own subnet.
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE
Typo in the book (page 473). The example 2001:db8:3c4d:1:0260:d6FF.FE73:1987/64 has a dot instead of a colon. A correct form is 2001:db8:3c4d:1:260:d6ff:fe73:1987/64. UPDATED (checked by script)
WARNING
Enabling IPv6 on an interface always creates a link-local address too. The global address is added to it, not instead of it.
Verifying addresses
Output from the book, shortened (illustrative, not run) CHECK
Corp# show ipv6 interface brief
FastEthernet0/0 [up/up]
FE80::20D:BDFF:FE3B:D80
FastEthernet0/1 [administratively down/down]
unassigned
- show ipv6 interface brief lists each interface with its status, link-local address and global address.
- show ipv6 interface fa0/0 gives full detail: addresses, joined multicast groups, DAD setting, ND timers. ADDED
Quick check 17.4.1
Q1. Which command makes a Cisco router forward IPv6 packets?
Answer: ipv6 unicast-routing - It is a global configuration command.
Q2. Which command gives an interface only a link-local address?
Answer: ipv6 enable - No global address is configured.
Q3. What does eui-64 at the end of ipv6 address do?
Answer: Builds the interface ID from the MAC address - You give only the prefix.
17.4.2 Stateless Autoconfiguration (eui-64)

Autoconfiguration lets a device give itself a link-local address and a global address. It learns the prefix from a router and builds the interface ID itself. It is called stateless because no server tracks which host got which address. BOOK
The EUI-64 interface ID

A MAC address is 48 bits but the interface ID is 64, so 16 bits are added. Modified EUI-64 does two things: insert FFFE in the middle (between the 3-byte OUI and the 3-byte device part) and flip the 7th bit of the first byte (the U/L bit). BOOK
- Write the MAC: 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E (OUI 001A2B, device part 3C4D5E).
- Insert FF:FE in the middle: 001A:2BFF:FE3C:4D5E.
- Flip the 7th bit of the first byte: 00 = 00000000 becomes 00000010 = 02.
- Result: 021A:2BFF:FE3C:4D5E, shortened 21a:2bff:fe3c:4d5e.
MEMORY TIP

Shortcut for the 7th bit: it is the same as XOR with 0x02, which changes only the second hex digit of the first byte: 0 to 2, 1 to 3, 2 to 0, 3 to 1, 4 to 6, 5 to 7, 6 to 4, 7 to 5, 8 to A, 9 to B, A to 8, B to 9, C to E, D to F, E to C, F to D.
| MAC | First byte in binary | Flipped | EUI-64 interface ID |
All eight results were calculated by script and agree with the book's own examples. CHECK only for the new rows because they are not from the book.
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

U/L bit wording. The book (Figure 17.4) says "10 = universally unique, 00 = locally unique", which is hard to follow. The clear version: in a normal MAC, bit value 0 means a burned-in (universally administered) address. EUI-64 inverts it, so in the interface ID 1 = universal and 0 = local. That is why most EUI-64 addresses show a 2 (or a 3, 6, 7, a, b, e, f depending on the OUI) where the MAC had a 0. UPDATED

Modern hosts often do not use EUI-64. Current Windows, Android, macOS and iOS generate random or temporary interface IDs for privacy. Cisco routers still use EUI-64 when you add eui-64, and the exam still tests it. ADDED General knowledge. CHECK
The two-step process (RS and RA)
- The host sends a router solicitation (RS) to FF02::2 (all routers). It is ICMPv6 type 133.
- The router answers with a router advertisement (RA) carrying the prefix. It goes to FF02::1 (all nodes), ICMPv6 type 134. RAs are also sent on a timer, but the RS gets an immediate answer.
EXAM CRITICAL
RS = 133 to FF02::2. RA = 134 to FF02::1. The advertised prefix must be /64 for SLAAC to work.
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

What is inside an RA ADDED : the prefix and its lifetimes, the A flag (autonomous: use SLAAC for this prefix), the M flag (managed: use stateful DHCPv6) and the O flag (other: use DHCPv6 for other settings like DNS), and router information used for the default gateway (the host uses the router's link-local address). On a Cisco router, ipv6 nd managed-config-flag sets M and ipv6 nd other-config-flag sets O. Sources: secondary (NetworkLessons-style articles, ipspace.net, NANOG). CHECK
After building its address the host runs duplicate address detection (see 17.4.5).
A router interface sends RAs only when ipv6 unicast-routing is on and RAs are not suppressed. CHECK
ipv6 address autoconfig (Branch router)
Book Figure 17.6 CHECK
Branch(config-if)# ipv6 address autoconfig default
- ipv6 address autoconfig makes the interface listen for RAs and build its own global address with EUI-64.
- default also installs the default route learned from the RA (the router that sent the RA becomes the gateway). The book says this correctly at page 476.
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

Contradiction at the end of the chapter. For the Boulder router (page 490) the book says the default keyword "will advertise itself as the default route for the local link". That is wrong: the keyword makes this router learn a default route from a neighbour's RA. It does not advertise anything. UPDATED CHECK Behaviour with ipv6 unicast-routing enabled depends on platform.
Quick check 17.4.2
Q1. What is the EUI-64 interface ID for MAC 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E?
Answer: 021a:2bff:fe3c:4d5e - Insert FFFE and flip the 7th bit (00 to 02). Calculated by script.
Q2. Which ICMPv6 type is a router advertisement?
Answer: B - 133 is RS, 135 NS, 136 NA.
Q3. Which multicast address does a host use for an RS?
Answer: FF02::2 - All routers on the link.
Q4. A MAC starts with 0A. What does the interface ID start with?
17.4.3 DHCPv6 (Stateful)

DHCPv6 works like DHCP for IPv4 but for IPv6 addresses. The book's main point: DHCP still matters because it can give options (DNS servers, domain name) that plain autoconfiguration, as the book describes it, does not. BOOK
| Method | Address from | Other settings (DNS) | RA flags |
| SLAAC only | The host, from the RA prefix | None (or from the RA itself, see below) | A=1, M=0, O=0 |
| SLAAC + stateless DHCPv6 | The host, from the RA prefix | DHCPv6 server | A=1, M=0, O=1 |
| Stateful DHCPv6 | DHCPv6 server (tracks leases) | DHCPv6 server | M=1 |
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

What the book gets wrong or leaves out. (1) It says that when no router is found the client sends a DHCP Solicit. In reality the RA flags (M and O) tell the host whether to use DHCPv6. The Solicit is a multicast to FF02::1:2, using UDP port 547 at the server and 546 at the client. (2) It says autoconfiguration has no way to carry DNS servers. Newer RA options can carry DNS servers and search lists; Cisco has ipv6 nd ra dns server on some platforms. (3) It says IOS DHCPv6 support is only stateless. Newer IOS releases can also run stateful pools. UPDATED Sources: secondary and general knowledge. CHECK
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)
DHCPv6 message order ADDED CHECK : Solicit, Advertise, Request, Reply (stateful). Stateless clients use Information-Request and Reply. Clients are identified by a DUID, not by MAC.
Stateless DHCPv6 server on Cisco IOS (example):
Stateless DHCPv6 (SLAAC for the address, DHCPv6 for DNS) ADDED CHECK
R1(config)# ipv6 dhcp pool LAN-POOL
R1(config-dhcpv6)# dns-server 2001:db8:acad:ffff::53
R1(config-dhcpv6)# domain-name example.com
R1(config-dhcpv6)# exit
R1(config)# interface g0/0
R1(config-if)# ipv6 dhcp server LAN-POOL
R1(config-if)# ipv6 nd other-config-flag
- ipv6 dhcp pool LAN-POOL creates a pool named LAN-POOL.
- dns-server and domain-name are the options handed out.
- ipv6 dhcp server LAN-POOL (interface) answers DHCPv6 requests on that LAN.
- ipv6 nd other-config-flag sets the O flag in RAs so hosts ask DHCPv6 for the options. To use a server on another subnet, use ipv6 dhcp relay destination <server address> on the LAN interface.
EXAM CRITICAL
Both stateless and stateful methods can give a host an IPv6 address dynamically. Stateless means no server tracks the address; stateful means a server does.
Quick check 17.4.3
Q1. Which RA flag tells hosts to use stateful DHCPv6?
Answer: M (managed) - O means other configuration only.
Q2. What destination address does a DHCPv6 Solicit use?

17.4.4 IPv6 Header

labs.title: Manual IPv6 addressing and static routes

content.text: - Build: PC1 to R1 g0/0, R1 g0/1 to R2 g0/1, R2 g0/0 to PC2. Plan: LAN A 2001:db8:acad:1::/64, link 2001:db8:acad:12::/64, LAN B 2001:db8:acad:2::/64.
- Configure R1 and R2 as below. Give the PCs static IPv6 addresses (PC1 2001:db8:acad:1::10, PC2 2001:db8:acad:2::10, both /64, gateway the router's ::1).
- Run the verification commands, then ping PC1 to PC2.
Commands CHECK
R1(config)# ipv6 unicast-routing
R1(config)# interface g0/0
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:acad:1::1/64
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# interface g0/1
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:acad:12::1/64
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# ipv6 route 2001:db8:acad:2::/64 2001:db8:acad:12::2
R2(config)# ipv6 unicast-routing
R2(config)# interface g0/1
R2(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:acad:12::2/64
R2(config-if)# no shutdown
R2(config-if)# interface g0/0
R2(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:acad:2::1/64
R2(config-if)# no shutdown
R2(config-if)# exit
R2(config)# ipv6 route 2001:db8:acad:1::/64 2001:db8:acad:12::1
R1# show ipv6 interface brief
R1# show ipv6 route
- ipv6 unicast-routing enables forwarding. no shutdown brings the interface up.
- ipv6 address .../64 sets the full address. The routers get a link-local address automatically.
- ipv6 route <prefix> <next hop> sends traffic for the far LAN to the other router.
MEMORY TIP

Expected result: show ipv6 interface brief lists a link-local (FE80::...) and your global address on each interface. show ipv6 route shows C for each connected /64, L /128 entries for the router's own addresses, and S 2001:DB8:ACAD:2::/64 [1/0] on R1. PC1 pings PC2 successfully. If not, check the return route on R2. CHECK
- On R1 remove the manual address on g0/0 and use EUI-64 instead.
- Before running show, find the MAC of g0/0 with show interfaces g0/0 (the burned-in address) and write down your predicted interface ID by hand.
- Compare your prediction with the router's address.
Commands CHECK
R1(config)# interface g0/0
R1(config-if)# no ipv6 address 2001:db8:acad:1::1/64
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:acad:1::/64 eui-64
R1# show interfaces g0/0
R1# show ipv6 interface brief
- no ipv6 address ... removes the manual address so the interface does not hold both.
- eui-64 builds the interface ID from the MAC.
- show interfaces g0/0 shows the MAC (bia). Use it to predict.
MEMORY TIP

Expected result: the global address is 2001:DB8:ACAD:1: followed by the EUI-64 of the g0/0 MAC, and the link-local address uses the same interface ID with the FE80:: prefix. If your prediction differs, check that you flipped the 7th bit and inserted FFFE in the middle. Update the PC default gateway if needed. CHECK
- Keep R1 g0/0 with a /64 global address and IPv6 routing on. Set PC1 to obtain IPv6 automatically (in Packet Tracer: IP Configuration, IPv6 Automatic).
- Look at the address the PC gets and compare it with the PC's MAC address.
- On R1 run show ipv6 interface g0/0.
MEMORY TIP

Expected result: the PC builds 2001:db8:acad:1:<interface ID> from the RA prefix and its own interface ID, and learns R1's link-local address as its gateway. In Packet Tracer the PC may use EUI-64 from its MAC; real modern hosts often use random interface IDs. Not every Packet Tracer version supports every RA behaviour. CHECK

labs.title: Floating static route and default route

content.text: - Add a second link: R1 g0/2 to R2 g0/2, with 2001:db8:acad:21::1/64 and ::2/64.
- On R1 keep the AD-1 route via 12::2 and add a floating static via 21::2 with AD 150. On R2 add a default route via 12::1.
- Run show ipv6 route static. Then shutdown R1 g0/1 and run it again. Ping PC2 from PC1 after each step.
- Bring g0/1 back with no shutdown and check again.
Commands CHECK
R1(config)# ipv6 route 2001:db8:acad:2::/64 2001:db8:acad:21::2 150
R2(config)# ipv6 route ::/0 2001:db8:acad:12::1
R1# show ipv6 route static
R1(config)# interface g0/1
R1(config-if)# shutdown
- The first command is the floating static route (AD 150, higher than the primary route's AD 1).
- The second command is a default route on R2 (stub network).
- shutdown on the primary link simulates a failure.
MEMORY TIP

Expected result: before the failure only the AD-1 route appears (S ... [1/0]). After the failure the AD-150 route appears (S ... [150/0]) and the ping still works. After no shutdown the AD-1 route returns. The return route on R2 needs to reach LAN A through whichever link is up: the default route via 12::1 stops working when g0/1 is down, so for a full test also give R2 a floating default through 21::1. CHECK
- On R1 run show ipv6 interface g0/0 and write down the joined groups.
- Compute the solicited-node multicast address from the last 24 bits of the global address and compare.
- Ping PC1 from R1, then run show ipv6 neighbors.
MEMORY TIP

Expected result: Joined group address(es) shows FF02::1, FF02::2 (routing on) and FF02::1:FFxx:xxxx where xx:xxxx are the last 24 bits of the address. After the ping, show ipv6 neighbors lists the PC with its MAC. Output format may differ in Packet Tracer. CHECK

labs.title: Lab 6 (optional): OSPFv3 instead of static routes

content.text: - Remove the static routes from Lab 1. Give R1 router ID 1.1.1.1 and R2 2.2.2.2.
- Enable OSPFv3 on g0/0 and g0/1 of both routers in area 0 (interface commands from Section 17.5).
- Verify with show ipv6 ospf neighbor and show ipv6 route ospf, then ping PC1 to PC2.
MEMORY TIP
Expected result: the neighbor shows state FULL, each router has an O route to the far LAN, and the ping works. Some Packet Tracer versions have limited OSPFv3 support. ADDED CHECK
Part A. EUI-64. Write the modified EUI-64 interface ID for each MAC. Then check below.
| MAC | Your answer | Correct answer (script) |
| 1E:00:5C:AA:BB:CC |  | 1c00:5cff:feaa:bbcc |
Part B. Shorten each address, then check.
| Full address | Shortest form (script) |
Part C. Expand fe80::a:b and 2001:db8:0:1::5.
MEMORY TIP
Part D. Classify each address.
| Address | Type (script) |
| 2001:db8:acad:1::1 | Global unicast range (documentation prefix) |
| fe80::1 | Link-local unicast |
| fd00:ab:cd::1 | Unique local |
| ff02::2 | Multicast (all routers) |
| ::1 | Loopback |
| 2a02:6b8::1 | Global unicast |
| fec0::1 | Site-local (deprecated) |
| ff02::1:ffab:cdef | Multicast (solicited-node) |
Part E. Subnetting. How many /64 subnets does a /48 contain? A /56? A /60? What is the next /64 after 2001:db8:acad:ff::/64?
MEMORY TIP

Answers (script): /48 contains 65,536 /64 subnets, a /56 contains 256, a /60 contains 16. The next /64 is 2001:db8:acad:100::/64 (the subnet field is hex, so ff + 1 = 100). Also: 2001:db8:acad:ffff::1 is inside 2001:db8:acad::/48; 2001:db8:acae::1 is not.

content.text: Q1 How many bits is an IPv6 address, and how many bits is an IPv4 address?
Answer: 128 and 32 - The IPv6 space is 2^96 times larger, not four times larger.
Q2 Roughly how many IPv6 addresses exist?
Answer: A - bout 3.4 x 10^38 - 2^128, calculated by script.
Q1 What replaces broadcast in IPv6?
A. Unicast only
B. Multicast (and anycast is new)
C. ARP
D. Nothing replaces it
Answer: B - There is no broadcast in IPv6.
Q2 How long is the basic IPv6 header?
Answer: 40 bytes, fixed - IPv4 is 20 bytes minimum and variable.
Q1 Is 2001::12::1234:56ab a legal address?
Answer: No - :: can be used only once.
Answer: fe80::204:61ff:fe9d:f156 - Drop leading zeros, then compress the one run of zero groups.
Q3 How many hex digits are in each group and how many bits?
Answer: 4 digits, 16 bits - Eight groups x 16 bits = 128 bits.
Q1 Which prefix is global unicast?
Answer: C - 2000::/3 (addresses starting with 2 or 3).
Q2 Can a router forward a packet whose destination is FE80::1?
Answer: No - Link-local is never routed off the link.
Q3 Which is the Layer 3 delivery model of anycast?
Answer: One-to-nearest - Not one-to-many.
Q4 What kind of address is fd12:3456:789a::1?
Answer: Unique local - It is inside FC00::/7 (script).
Q1 What is the IPv6 loopback address?
Answer: ::1 - There is only one loopback address.
Q2 Which prefix should you use in documentation and labs?
Answer: 2001:db8::/32 - Never real prefixes. 3fff::/20 is also reserved.
Q1 Which command makes a Cisco router forward IPv6 packets?
Answer: ipv6 unicast-routing - It is a global configuration command.
Q2 Which command gives an interface only a link-local address?
Answer: ipv6 enable - No global address is configured.
Q3 What does eui-64 at the end of ipv6 address do?
Answer: B - uilds the interface ID from the MAC address - You give only the prefix.
Q1 What is the EUI-64 interface ID for MAC 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E?
Answer: 021a:2bff:fe3c:4d5e - Insert FFFE and flip the 7th bit (00 to 02). Calculated by script.
Q2 Which ICMPv6 type is a router advertisement?
Answer: B - 133 is RS, 135 NS, 136 NA.
Q3 Which multicast address does a host use for an RS?
Answer: FF02::2 - All routers on the link.
Q4 A MAC starts with 0A. What does the interface ID start with?
Q1 Which RA flag tells hosts to use stateful DHCPv6?
Answer: M (managed) - O means other configuration only.
Q2 What destination address does a DHCPv6 Solicit use?
Answer: FF02::1:2 - All DHCPv6 relay agents and servers.
Q1 What is the IPv6 equivalent of the IPv4 TTL field?
Answer: Hop Limit - Reduced by one at every router.
Q2 Who fragments an IPv6 packet?
Answer: The sending host, never a router - Routers send a Packet Too Big message instead.
Q3 Which header field was removed completely?
A. Hop Limit
B. Header checksum
C. Version
D. Source address
Answer: B - Upper layers and Layer 2 check for errors.
Q1 Which Next Header value identifies ICMPv6?
Answer: 58 - 6 is TCP and 17 is UDP.
Q2 What replaces ARP in IPv6?
Answer: Neighbor discovery (NS and NA) - Carried in ICMPv6.
Q3 What is the solicited-node multicast address for a host whose address ends ...:fe18:fc0f?
Answer: FF02::1:FF18:FC0F - FF02::1:FF plus the last 24 bits.
Q4 Which message does a router send when a packet is too big for the next link?
Answer: ICMPv6 Packet Too Big (type 2) - The source then lowers its packet size.
Q1 Which version of OSPF is used for IPv6?
Answer: OSPFv3 - OSPF for IPv4 is OSPFv2.
Q2 How do you enable OSPFv3 on an interface?
Answer: ipv6 ospf <process> area <area> on the interface - There are no network statements.
Q1 What is the IPv6 default route?
Answer: ::/0 - The same idea as 0.0.0.0/0.
Q2 What makes a static route floating?
Answer: A - higher administrative distance than the primary route - It only appears in the routing table if the primary disappears.
Q3 When must you add the exit interface to a static route with a next hop?
Answer: When the next hop is a link-local address - Link-local addresses are only unique per link.
Q1 What does an L entry in show ipv6 route mean?
Answer: A - local /128 route for the router's own interface address - C is the connected prefix; L is the router's own address.
Q2 Why does ipv6 address 2001:db8:3c4d:12::/64 without eui-64 trigger a warning?
Answer: The interface ID is all zeros, the subnet-router anycast address - Add eui-64 or a host part.
Q3 Should both ends of a router-to-router link use the same /64?
Answer: Yes - They share one subnet, with different interface IDs.
Q1 Which route is used when both an AD 150 static route and an OSPF route exist for the same prefix?
Answer: The OSPF route - OSPF AD 110 is lower than 150.
Q2 Why do the book's pings from Corp succeed even though SF and LA have few routes?
Answer: The ping source is the directly connected outgoing interface address - The far router has a connected route back to it.
Q1 How many bits is an IPv6 address, and how is it written?
Answer: 128 bits, as eight groups of four hex digits separated by colons - Each group is 16 bits.
Answer: 2001:db8::12:0:0:1 - Compress the first of two equal-length runs of zero groups. (script)
Q3 Which address is valid?
Answer: B - A has two ::, C has too few groups, D has an invalid hex digit g.
Q4 What is the modified EUI-64 interface ID of MAC 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E?
Answer: 021a:2bff:fe3c:4d5e - Insert FFFE and flip the 7th bit. (script)
Q5 What is the EUI-64 interface ID of MAC FC:99:47:75:CE:E0?
Answer: fe99:47ff:fe75:cee0 - fc = 11111100 becomes 11111110 = fe. (script)
Q6 A MAC starts with 3C. What does its EUI-64 interface ID start with?
A. 3C
B. 3D
C. 3E
D. 3F
Answer: C - 3C = 00111100, flip the 7th bit: 00111110 = 3E.
Q7 Which prefix is link-local unicast?
Answer: B - FE80::/10 covers fe80:: to febf::.
Q8 Which prefix range does 2000::/3 cover?
Answer: 2000:: to 3fff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff - Addresses beginning with 2 or 3. (script)
Q9 What kind of address is fd12:3456:789a::1?
Answer: Unique local - It lies inside FC00::/7. (script)
Q10 What is the IPv6 loopback address and what is the unspecified address?
Answer: ::1 and :: - Equivalent to 127.0.0.1 and 0.0.0.0.
Q11 Name the three IPv6 communication types.
Answer: Unicast, multicast, anycast - There is no broadcast.
Q12 An anycast packet is delivered to...
A. Every device with the address
B. The nearest device with the address
C. One random device
D. Only the router
Answer: B - One-to-nearest.
Q13 Which multicast address do hosts use for a router solicitation, and which ICMPv6 type is it?
Answer: FF02::2, type 133 - All routers on the link.
Q14 Which multicast address does a router advertisement go to, and which type is it?
Answer: FF02::1, type 134 - All nodes on the link.
Q15 Which prefix length must an advertised SLAAC prefix have?
Answer: /64 - The interface ID is 64 bits.
Q16 RA flags are A=1, M=0, O=1. Which method is this?
Answer: SLAAC for the address and stateless DHCPv6 for other settings (such as DNS) - M=1 would mean stateful DHCPv6.
Q17 What is the solicited-node multicast address for 2001:db8:acad:1:21a:2bff:fe3c:4d5e?
Answer: ff02::1:ff3c:4d5e - FF02::1:FF plus the last 24 bits. The Ethernet MAC is 33:33:ff:3c:4d:5e. (script)
Q18 How long is the IPv6 basic header and how large is the Flow Label field?
Answer: 40 bytes; 20 bits - The book says 24 bits, which is wrong.
Q19 Which IPv6 header field replaces the IPv4 TTL?
Answer: Hop Limit - It is reduced by 1 at every router.
Q20 Which Next Header value identifies ICMPv6?
Answer: C - 6 = TCP, 17 = UDP, 58 = ICMPv6.
Q21 What replaces ARP in IPv6?
Answer: Neighbor discovery using ICMPv6 NS and NA - Types 135 and 136.
Q22 How many DAD neighbor solicitations does a host normally send by default?
Answer: One - The book says three, which is out of date. CHECK default is configurable.
Q23 What command lets a Cisco router forward IPv6 packets?
Answer: ipv6 unicast-routing - Global configuration.
Q24 You type ipv6 address 2001:db8:acad:5::/64 on a router interface and get a subnet router anycast warning. Why?
Answer: The interface ID is all zeros - Use eui-64 or add a host part.
Q25 What does the L entry mean in show ipv6 route?
Answer: A - local /128 route for the router's own address - The book wrongly calls it the link-local address.
Q26 Write the IPv6 default route.
Answer: ipv6 route ::/0 <next hop or interface> - It matches everything.
Q27 What makes a static route a floating static route?
Answer: A - higher administrative distance than another route to the same prefix - For example AD 150 against OSPF 110.
Q28 Which three migration methods move a network from IPv4 to IPv6?
Answer: D - ual stack, tunnelling, translation - Dual stack is the most common.
